content: 1. Performance bias was identified due to the lack of blinding in the trials. This limitation was noted and considered in the analysis. 2. In single trials, inconsistency could not be evaluated, and therefore, the evidence was downgraded once. 3. The original sample size in some studies did not accurately represent the effective cluster-adjusted sample size used in the meta-analysis. 4. Three trials (Jamil, 2017; Katz, 2018; MacGowan, 2017) were included in the meta-analysis. All trials were conducted among men who have sex with men (MSM) in high-income countries, specifically Australia and the United States. 5. Three individual randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were included, and the evidence was downgraded once. 6. The meta-analysis showed consistent beneficial effects across individual RCTs, with no significant differences observed in other critical outcomes. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) determined that downgrading for inconsistency was unnecessary. 7. In the meta-analysis, studies by Choko (2019a) and Wray (2018) included more than one intervention arm with similar HIV self-testing (HIVST) kit distribution methods. Therefore, all intervention arms were combined. However, in studies by Chanda (2017) and Ortblad (2017), the HIVST kit distribution methods differed, so intervention arms were not combined. Adjustments were made to the control arm sample to prevent double counting. 8. Cluster-adjusted analyses were included in the meta-analysis for cluster-randomized trials. 9. Eleven individual randomized trials and six cluster-randomized trials were included in the analysis. 10. Evidence was downgraded once due to a 4% overall loss to follow-up (LTFU), with 26% in the intervention arm and 50% in the control arm. Three cluster-randomized trials were subject to potential recruitment bias. 11. Several risk of bias domains were classified as unclear due to insufficient information from unpublished reports or conference abstracts. 12. Outcome definitions were inconsistent across trials. Eight trials defined positivity as a confirmed HIV diagnosis, while others reported reactive HIVST results as positive, relied on self-reported positivity, or had unclear definitions. 13. One trial (Nichols, 2019) reported significantly lower HIV positivity among those tested in the intervention arm. This trial focused on young people in a setting with high testing coverage. 14. Six trials were conducted among MSM, three among male partners of antenatal care (ANC) women, and two among male truck drivers. Sub-analyses among men were included. 15. Three trials were conducted among female sex workers, and one sub-analysis among women was included. 16. Two trials were conducted among young people, and two others presented sub-analyses among young people. 17. Evidence was downgraded twice due to potential performance bias (lack of blinding) in all trials, detection bias (self-reported or non-validated outcomes) in some trials, and unclear risk of detection bias in one trial. 18. Three of four trials had more than three high-risk or unclear risk of bias domains. 19. In some trials, the original sample size did not represent the effective cluster-adjusted sample size used in the meta-analysis. 20. In studies by Wray (2018), Chanda (2017), and Ortblad (2017), intervention arms were not pooled due to differences in the intervention package, which could impact positivity rates. Adjustments were made to prevent double counting. 21. In studies by Choko (2019a) and Wray (2018), intervention arms with similar HIVST kit distribution methods were combined. However, in Choko (2019b), two intervention arms with different sub-groups (ANC women and ART clients) were combined, but sub-groups were presented separately. 22. One cluster-randomized trial was subject to recruitment bias, and all trials had unclear risk of selection bias. Three of four trials had more than three high-risk or unclear risk of bias domains. 23. Outcome definitions were inconsistent across trials. Some trials defined positivity as confirmed HIV-positive diagnosis, while others relied on self-reported positivity or unclear definitions. 24. In studies by Chanda (2017) and Ortblad (2017), only the HIVST arm with facility-based HIVST distribution was included in the analysis.
